items.a: A FormGroup is used to group multiple form controls into a single object and manage their values, validation, and status together.

items.q: setValue() vs patchValue() in Angular FormGroup.
items.a:
1)setValue() updates all controls in the FormGroup. You must provide values for every control.


2)patchValue() updates only the controls you specify. Other controls remain unchanged.

items.q: What are the new template syntax changes in Angular?
items.a:
Angular 17 introduced a new feature called Built-in Control Flow. It provides a new way to write conditions, loops, and switch statements directly inside Angular templates.
Previously, Angular used structural directives such as *ngIf, *ngFor, and ngSwitch. Now, we can use @if, @for, and @switch.

One important difference is that the new syntax is not a directive. It is built-in control flow syntax provided by Angular.

items.q: Why was the new syntax introduced?
items.a:
- To make Angular templates cleaner and easier to read.
- To reduce the need for structural directives for common control-flow operations.
- To handle conditions and loops directly inside templates.
-To improve list rendering with the track expression.
-To avoid importing CommonModule just for these built-in control-flow features.

items.q: Difference between track and trackBy in Angular
items.a:
Both track and trackBy help Angular identify list items and minimize unnecessary DOM updates when a collection changes.

The main difference is that track is used with the new @for syntax, whereas trackBy is used with the older *ngFor syntax.

When iterating over a collection of data using *ngFor, the code works even if we don't provide trackBy. However, using trackBy is recommended for better performance because it helps Angular identify items efficiently.

In the new @for syntax, providing a track expression is mandatory. If we don't provide it, Angular will throw an error, and the @for block will not work.

Another difference is that with *ngFor, we generally need to define a trackBy function in the TypeScript file, whereas with @for, we can directly provide a tracking expression in the template without creating a separate function in the TypeScript file.

These are built-in contextual variables available inside Angular's @for loop. They help you identify an item's position in a list.

$index: Display serial numbers in a table.
$first: Highlight the first item.
$last: Add a special style to the last item.
$even and $odd: Apply alternate row colors in a table (zebra striping).

- Interface: Defines the structure of an object. It tells TypeScript what properties an object should have and their types.
- Generic: Makes functions, classes and other reusable structures work with different data types while maintaining type safety.
Interface defines the shape of data. Generic allows us to reuse code with different types of data.
Product[], User[] and Challan[] are the types defined using interfaces.
T is the generic parameter that accepts whichever type we provide.

A Type Alias allows us to give a custom name to a type so that we can reuse it wherever required.
In simple words: Instead of writing the same type repeatedly, we create a name for it using type.
Suppose you have a variable that accepts either a number or a string.
Type Alias can also represent union types, primitive types, tuples and more.
A Tuple is a special type of array where we define the type of each element and its position in advance.

notes.js-template-literals:
Strings

Template literals

Template literals are a way to create strings in JavaScript using backticks (`) instead of single quotes (' ') or double quotes (" ").

They make it easier to:

1. Insert variables into strings using ${}.

2. Write strings across multiple lines.

3. Perform expressions directly inside strings.

const name = 'Ram';
const msg = `Hello ${name}, you have ${3 + 2} new messages`;

const html = `
  <div class="card">
    <h2>${name}</h2>
  </div>`;

Tagged templates pass the string parts and values to a function first, e.g. html`<p>${x}</p>` in some libraries, to escape or process values.
notes.js-promise-combinators:
Async

Promise.all, allSettled, race & any

Promise.all() — Returns results when all Promises succeed; rejects if any Promise fails.

Promise.allSettled() — Waits for all Promises to finish and returns the status and result of each Promise, whether successful or failed.

Promise.race() — Returns the result of the first Promise to settle, whether it succeeds or fails.

Promise.any() — Returns the result of the first Promise to succeed; rejects with an AggregateError if all Promises fail.





 
const [users, products] = await Promse.all([
  fetch('/api/users').then(r => r.json()),
  fetch('/api/products').then(r => r.json())
]);

const results = await Promise.allSettled([saveA(), saveB()]);
const failed = results.filter(r => r.status === 'rejected');

const report = await Promise.race([
  fetch('/api/report'),
  new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('Timeout')), 5000))
]);
RxJS equivalents: Promise.all is like forkJoin; Promise.race is like race.
notes.angular-cli:
Tooling

What is Angular CLI?

Angular CLI is a command-line tool used to create, run, build, and manage Angular applications using commands, instead of writing everything manually.

  • Automates development tasks like generating components, services, and modules, and building the project.
